The first time I noticed time was lying, it was on a clock that didn’t tick the way it promised. It sat above a kitchen doorway, painted the color of old bones, and it had been there long enough that no one remembered when it had been set. Everyone treated it like furniture. You could walk past it every day and never look twice, except that one morning—because mornings always arrive with an unexpected sharpness—I stood still and watched the second hand hesitate, as if it were deciding whether to continue.

It didn’t stop. It didn’t jump. It simply seemed to consider the next motion, then commit. And I realized: even the most mechanical things could be persuading you, could be shaping your sense of what counts as “now.” We believe in clocks because clocks behave. We believe in calendars because calendars repeat. But behavior is not proof. Repetition is not truth. A clock can be right and still be misleading. A calendar can be correct and still ignore the weather in your life.

That was the morning I began collecting small betrayals of certainty. Not in any dramatic way—no notes pinned to a wall, no dramatic epiphanies. Just an attention that grew teeth.

The cashier at the corner store told me the card reader was “being difficult,” and I watched their fingers punch numbers with confidence while their eyes avoided mine. Difficulty is a soft word. It makes the problem sound like a shy animal. Later, I saw another customer swipe and succeed in a single try. The machine wasn’t difficult. The story was. The story was what they needed in the moment to keep moving, to keep their own hands from trembling under the counter.

I started thinking about how many lies we do not call lies. We call them politeness, optimism, habit. We call them “just how it is.” We call them “being careful,” even when careful means smoothing the edge of reality so it doesn’t cut anyone immediately. There are times when a lie is just a bandage. There are times when a lie is an operating theater.

Maybe all of us live inside some arrangement of bandages and operating theaters, depending on who’s watching and how much time we have.

I don’t remember deciding to notice this. It was like learning a new color. Once you can name it, you keep seeing it everywhere. The world doesn’t change; your gaze does. Or maybe your gaze changes the world, because the world responds. Even objects seem more reactive once you begin treating them as participants instead of scenery.

In the park, the fountain always ran, even when the water looked thin, even when the algae on the edge smelled faintly metallic. A man sat on the bench with a paper cup and a newspaper folded too neatly, like he was practicing calm. A teenager circled him on a bicycle, pretending not to see. The teenager’s friends laughed too loudly. Then, at some point, laughter became quiet without anybody acknowledging the shift. When it did, the man glanced at the ground as if checking whether the earth had moved under him.

Time again. The way it stretches in the absence of permission. The way it contracts when you’re sure you’ll be watched.

I wondered what the teenager was thinking. I wondered what the man had lost. I wondered whether either of those thoughts would matter to the other. The fountain kept running. Leaves kept collecting in the same corners. Nothing dramatic happened. Nothing resolved. And yet, in that refusal to resolve, something became strangely bright. I felt a kind of tenderness toward the ordinary. It wasn’t comforting, exactly. It was more like acknowledging a fact about weather: the wind will not apologize. It will not explain itself. It will simply keep coming.

So I learned to stop demanding narration from my days.

There was a stretch of time—weeks, maybe—when I felt as though I was living inside other people’s sentences. I’d catch myself finishing someone else’s thought. I’d walk into a room and guess what the conversation was about before anyone said it. My mind seemed to fit itself into patterns I hadn’t chosen, like a key that was shaped for a lock somewhere else.

Then one afternoon, I forgot. I stood in a hallway holding a bag of groceries, and I couldn’t remember whether I’d already gone to the store. The knowledge was there, like a window behind frosted glass, but it wouldn’t clear. I tried to remember the smell of the place, the sound of coins in a pocket. Nothing solid came.

At first I panicked—not loudly, not with drama, but in that inward way panic has, like an electrical fault traveling down a wire. I set the bag on the floor. My hands went empty. For a moment I felt my body and not my thoughts. I listened for footsteps in the house, for the hum of the fridge, for the small noises that prove you’re still inside the world. They were there. Everything was normal.

Then the memory arrived in a rush, not as a tidy story but as fragments: the coldness of oranges, the cashier’s voice, a song from the radio I didn’t like but couldn’t stop hearing. It all fit together with a click that felt too satisfying for something that had almost scared me. I realized I hadn’t been forgetting time—I’d been forgetting permission. I’d been trying to remember in a way that didn’t work, because the way you remember is not always the same way you live.

That’s when I started wondering whether we are always living one version of ourselves ahead of ourselves.

There are people who talk as if they’re already finished. They speak in endings. They announce what they will and will not do, like their lives are completed jigsaws waiting only for the last piece. Their certainty has a certain beauty, like polished stone. It shines. But if you touch it, it can be too smooth. Smoothness can be a way of avoiding the sharp edges of growth.

Other people seem to live under constant revision. They make plans, then change them. They say “I don’t know yet” as if it were a place they keep. Sometimes it’s an escape. Sometimes it’s a strategy for staying flexible in a world that refuses to hold still. Sometimes it’s wisdom.

I don’t know which kind I am. I only know I am always learning which kind I need to be in order to survive whatever is happening next.

Because what is happening next is never just the next thing. It’s the next thing plus your history. It’s the next thing filtered through all the things you’ve already believed. It’s the next thing with your fear sitting on top like a heavy suitcase.

I think that’s why the smallest betrayals of certainty matter. They remind you that you’re not an equation. You’re not a machine. You’re not a clock that can be trusted because it keeps moving. You’re an animal made of meaning, and meaning is not stable. Meaning depends on breath, on light, on the angle of a sentence someone says to you in passing.

Once, in a bookstore, I watched a woman pick up a book and hold it against her chest. She didn’t buy it. She didn’t read it. She just stood there for a long time, as if the book were an object that had weight beyond its pages. When she finally put it back, her face looked newly emptied, like she’d taken something out and put it somewhere else inside herself. She left. The store remained.

The book stayed where it always stays: on a shelf waiting for whoever might need it. But in the moment, the book was no longer a book. It was a vessel. It was a permission slip. It was a substitute for a conversation she couldn’t have. I walked through the aisles after she left and felt oddly grateful. Grateful not because everything worked out, but because there was evidence that people use objects to carry hope without announcing it.

Hope is often quiet. It doesn’t always arrive with fanfare. It shows up as a second cup of coffee you’re willing to make. It shows up as putting on a coat even though you don’t feel like going anywhere. It shows up as the decision to answer a message, to try again, to look up.

And sometimes hope is the decision to notice that time is lying—not that it is false, but that it is incomplete. A clock can measure movement while ignoring meaning. A calendar can count days while ignoring grief. A schedule can tell you what happens while missing how it feels.

So I started treating time like a neighbor instead of a judge.

I began asking myself questions that didn’t demand immediate answers: What am I avoiding? What am I rushing? What am I pretending doesn’t matter because it would take too long to think about? Who do I become when I’m not performing certainty?

There are nights when I still look at the clock above the doorway and watch the second hand hesitate, that small moment of reconsideration. I don’t feel alarm anymore. I feel invitation. I feel reminded that even the most reliable things have micro-movements we barely notice, that even the most predictable sequences contain pauses.

If time is lying, it’s not trying to hurt me. It’s simply refusing to be everything at once. It can only be what it can be: a tool. A signal. A rhythm.

And I—messy, human, always half-made—can be something else besides a machine that insists on accuracy. I can be, at least sometimes, the one who listens for the truth beneath the surface: not in the numbers, but in the way a day shifts when you finally let yourself see it.
